source: As we descend, we’ll encounter 138 people.
why: Counts the people in the dataset, a data-size description rather than a finding drawn from the data.

source: We sifted through over three years of Wikipedia pageview data
why: Describes the collection period, not a result computed from the files.

source: There were eight levels (like Karate belts): (1) 50, (2) 100, (3) 200, (4) 500, (5) 1,000, (6) 2,000, (7) 5,000, and (8) 10,000, pageviews.
why: The thresholds are methodology inputs. The data also contains levels 0 and 9 outside the eight named thresholds, so the exact eight-level scheme is not a computed result.

source: a foundation of over 40,000 people
why: Describes the source population used to build the list; the file contains only the 138 selected people.

source: Any person who appeared in the top 1,000 pages for at least one day in that range was considered.
why: Describes data collection, not a finding computed from the files.

source: After assigning levels, anyone with 1. a beginning level lower than 4, 2. a level change of more than 4 levels, and 3. less than level 2 in 2015, was included in the final list.
why: Inclusion criteria/methodology, not a result; the provided file is already the filtered final list.

source: If someone hit a new level of pageviews and never dipped below that level’s threshold again, they were assigned the level, hence the term “sustained pageviews.”
why: Defines the level-assignment method, not a result; the provided level column is already assigned.

source: Higher up means more accumulated pageviews, further down means less.
why: Describes the chart's vertical encoding rather than a result; the underlying cumulative ranking is used in other facts.

source: more towards to the left means a faster ascent to popularity.
why: Describes the chart's horizontal encoding; the files do not contain the chart's x coordinate.

source: 93 of the top 100 most-viewed videos of all-time are music videos.
why: External YouTube statistic, not present in the two Wikipedia pageview files.

source: Dua Lipa rose to fame with the song “New Rules,” which has 1.5 billion views on YouTube.
why: YouTube view count is external; the files contain Wikipedia pageviews, not video views.

source: According to her Wikipedia page, the 23-year-old English singer started posting covers to her channel at 14.
why: Age and YouTube history are not fields in the data; the extract only mentions starting at 14, not being 23.

source: Rapper 6ix9ine is the first overnight success based on Wikipedia traffic.
why: The 'first overnight success' ranking is qualitative; no story-defined measure of overnight success is in the files. The verifiable late-debut pattern is included separately.

source: his page was created after he started to become quite popular.
why: Wikipedia page-creation dates are not in the files; only monthly pageview records are.

source: They are highly controversial but have a massive presence with over 35 million followers combined.

source: New Netflix series have definitely contributed to putting a lot of new actors in the spotlight.
